#1416. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR

It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

The visitors needed something special to get back into it and it came from the most unlikely of sources as Botman unleashed a rocket from 25 yards.

Sven Botman, that is SENSATIONAL! 🤯 https://t.co/GalkqMs5ZE

In a flash the balance of play shifted in Newcastle’s favour. They poured forward in search of the equaliser. Jaissle switched to a 4-4-2 with Will Osula joining Fernandez-Pardo up front, but instead of pulling level, Coventry pulled further ahead.

"We need to improve the things we can control, and right now that's a lot" 🗣️ Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle expresses his disappointment after his side's loss to Coventry 👇 https://t.co/fatJkZYyRM

Very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. We know we are going to have to suffer this season, when we don’t have a lot of the ball. We have to understand it. The level is what it is.

The work ethic, the belief. You get what you deserve. Great finishes. We haven’t quite had the rub of the green this season and that might have helped us nick a couple of more points. I’m a firm believer that you keep going. It was a complete performance. We’ve got to keep our feet on the ground because we’re going to have to do 30+ of those but it’s a great feeling for the players.

[Cherif] is very, very exciting because he is so young. He has got a really good manner. He wants to train, he wants to learn. He’s quite quiet but on the pitch he shows a lot of personality. When you see the quality of the strike and the hold-up play, there’s a lot to come from him.

The first two minutes of stoppage time, of which there are four, pass without incident.

Osula lifts a volley over the bar with a wild attempt. Toure was injured in the build-up and will be replaced by Dan Burn.

The first was baffling as the Belgium international made no attempt to sweep in Jacob Murphy’s cutback at the near post, letting it run through his legs thinking Harvey Barnes was in a better position. He wasn’t.

The second was a little unfortunate as he did well to time his run and wriggle free of centre back Bobby Thomas. That put him in on goal with just the goalkeeper to beat, but having sat Chris Rushworth down he pushed the ball a fraction too wide and by the time he was in a position to shoot, Thomas had done brilliantly to cut off the angle and block it.

Coventry have been good but Newcastle have been really poor again away from home. They are yet to put a 90-minute performance together since the opening weekend against Liverpool. Matthias Jaissle will want a lot more from his team in the second half.

Newcastle should at least be level given their chances but you have to admire Coventry’s spirit and work rate. Cherif seems to me to have a high ceiling and at 19 is already a real handful.

Newcastle need to stop fannying around and buy a proper centre-forward. Wissa is better wide or in a more fluid system, as I suspect Fernandez-Pardo is, too. Stick Osula on and get the chequebook out in January. Offer Boro £50m for Lankshear.

Cheeif, working his socks off, chases a lost cause and retrieves a long pass forward in the whitewash but when he turns to try to play it to Thomas-Asante, Thiaw makes a good tackle.

Hall turns away Mason-Clark’s effort from the left and the game turns into a basketball match… without the scoring as both sides fly from end to end.  Two minutes of stoppage time to come.

Thomas to the rescue again, He was outpaced by Fernandez-Pardo running on to straight ball down the middle but kept on going when the Belgium forward rounded the keeper to block the shot. Fernandez-Pardo may have been better off taking on the shot earlier, surprising the advancing Rushworth, rather than trying to take him out of the equation. Or dinked it before he got too close.

Newcastle force Coventry all the way back to Rushworth who knocks it long to Dasilva who holds it up well and passes to Mason-Clark. The left-winger runs and then tries to force the ball through Thiaw instead of laying it back to the left-back who was free. Thiaw makes the block.

Hornicek, rushed into a clearance, makes haste to belt it away from danger.

End to end after Fernandez-Pardo at the near post is in the right position to hook in a shot from Murphy’s cross but he dummies instead and there was no one behind him. Was he put off by a defender’s shout? Coventry break and storm down the inside-right, Cherif closing in on goal and refusing the entreaties of Mason-Clark and Rudoni to pass inside. he shoots straight at Hornicek.

Newcastle think they should have a corner and they are right after Van Ewijk’s block of Fernandez-Pardo’s cross took a double deflection back off the Coventry right-back. To set up that raid down the wing, Willock bullied Yirenkyi off the ball on halfway.

Coventry break the siege with a clearance that allows Mason-Clark to shield the ball and buy a throw-in on the left. The ref warns Van Ewijk not to take too long over it after taking his time to jog over from the other wing.

Coventry are playing a dangerous game now and Newcastle have all the momentum, stringing passes together and using their wide players well.

Barnes sticks out his right foot in the Coventry box and steers a shot wide from Willock’s cross/shot. Thomas had earlier intercepted Murphy’s dipping cross to nod it away from Fernandez-Pardo as Coventry retreat.

Barnes passes blind back to Hornicek unaware that Cherif was lurking. But the Czech goalkeeper is more alert and darts out to clear.

Botman, who has never looked the same since his injury, heads the ball out for a throw-in. Barnes is in space to his left but he chops to his right, looking for an opportunity to shoot but can’t find one then forces a pass beyond Murphy who had left his wing. Coventry pick it off but butcher the counter-attack with a rubbish pass to Cherif that was off target.

Thomas, the right-sided centre-back, strides out of defence and sees Cherif loitering on Botman’s shoulder but overhits his pass down the inside-right channel.

Hall sends Fernandez-Pardo down the left and the forward retrieves it just by the byline. He cuts it back to Willock who spins to tee up Barnes to fire a left-foot daisy-cutter from 18 yards straight at Rushworth.

Terrible goalkeeping from Lukasz Hornicek who made one mistake and followed it up with another diving at full stretch at the feet of a Coventry player in the box. He did not need to go after the ball as there was no imminent danger.

Sidiki Cherif knew he only needed to get a touch on it before the Newcastle goalkeeper. Such a soft penalty to give away early on away from home.

Newcastle have not started the game well but the goalkeeper will have a lot of explaining to do after that one

A flag catches Barnes offside. Slow start from the visitors.

Hornicke made a dog’s dinner of that. A headlong dive to try to recover his clumsy handling and Cherif beat him to it. Hotnicek swiped across his ankles and it was a stuck on penalty.

Mistake by Hornicek and then he appears to bring down Cherif diving to retrieve it.

Good atmosphere. The home fans are making a racket.

As the strains of We’ll Live and Die in These Towns dies down to segue into the Eton Boating Song, Newcastle kick off, attacking from right to left. When they lose the ball Wissa is penalised for tripping Rudoni 45 yards out.

Coventry are in blue and white stripes, harking back to the 1987 Cup final rather than the Mick Coop years. Newcastle are in vibrant lilac.

It was good to get a win. We worked very hard for it. It’s so hard to get wins, especially on the road. And now we’re back at home and we have to work on those attributes [that earned us the win] at Forest. We rotated pretty well, there are different aspects of the game we want to improve on regardless of shape.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1415. This cholesterol drug promised to be a game-changer. Why did it flop in the clinic — and is there still hope?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Cassandra Willyard is a science journalist in Madison, Wisconsin.

Lipoprotein(a) is a cholesterol-carrying molecule that raises the risk of cardiovascular disease. Credit: Juan Gaertner/Science Photo Library

In early September, pharmaceutical giant Novartis issued a press release that sent shock waves through the cardiology community. A drug called pelacarsen, once expected to be a potential blockbuster, had failed to reduce the risk of heart problems and stroke in people with underlying cardiovascular disease.

More muscle, less belly fat: mutations to a gene are linked to wide-ranging benefits

More muscle, less belly fat: mutations to a gene are linked to wide-ranging benefits

Michelle O’Donoghue, a cardiologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, Massachusetts, says her initial reaction to the news was “a state of disbelief”.

Pelacarsen lowers the levels of a type of cholesterol-carrying molecule called lipoprotein(a), often referred to as Lp(a) or Lp little a. Similar to low-density lipoprotein, or LDL, high levels of Lp(a) increase the risk of heart attacks and other heart-related problems. But unlike LDL (sometimes called bad cholesterol), Lp(a) levels are determined mostly by genetics, rather than lifestyle. So, the roughly one in five people who have high Lp(a) levels cannot reduce them through changes in diet and exercise. And although people can lower their LDL levels with statins and other medications, there are no approved drugs that substantially lower Lp(a).

That is why cardiologists were so excited about pelacarsen and a handful of other Lp(a)-lowering drugs that are currently in late-stage clinical trials. “Lp(a) has really been the talk of the town over the past several years in the cardiovascular community, in part because of a lot of enthusiasm over these therapies,” says O’Donoghue, who is an investigator on one of the trials. The therapies lower Lp(a) by 80% or more. All researchers had to prove was that this reduction leads to better clinical outcomes — fewer heart-related deaths, heart attacks, strokes and emergency bypass surgeries.

Why the trial, known as Lp(a)HORIZON, failed isn’t yet clear (see go.nature.com/4sv4ekx). Novartis representatives did not reply to a request for comments. But the high-profile miss has cardiologists questioning what they know about the relationship between Lp(a) and major heart-related problems, and wondering whether other Lp(a)-lowering therapies will meet a similar fate. The US drug firms Amgen and Eli Lilly have large trials under way to test therapies that target Lp(a) using a different approach.

“We had hoped that this would be the first step into a big new area of therapy,” says Harpreet Bhatia, a cardiologist at the University of California, San Diego. Now, he and other researchers are awaiting further details on the Novartis trial and the results from other trials to see whether there is still a future for such approaches to reducing Lp(a).

Lp(a) and LDL both carry cholesterol, a fatty substance that is produced mostly in the liver. The body needs cholesterol, but when its levels are high, it can be deposited in artery walls and form hard plaques, a process known as atherosclerosis. These plaques can grow so thick that they choke off blood flow or rupture, causing blood clots that can prompt a heart attack.

Study after study has shown that people with higher Lp(a) levels are at greater risk of coronary events such as heart attacks, heart-valve problems and heart failure than are individuals with lower levels1. And over the past 30 years, genetic data have bolstered the idea that Lp(a) is not just a marker of risk, but also a causal factor2. “Genetically, I don’t think you could ask for better evidence for this as a drug target,” says Børge Nordestgaard, a cardiologist at the University of Copenhagen and president of the European Atherosclerosis Society in Gothenburg, Sweden.

Structurally, Lp(a) isn’t much different from LDL. Both are essentially globs of fat surrounded by a protein called apolipoprotein B (see ‘Stopping lipoprotein(a)’). Both are produced in the liver. There is, however, one major difference. Lp(a) has a tail composed of apolipoprotein(a), which loops in segments called ‘kringles’ — named after the twists of a Scandinavian pastry. Lp(a) levels depend, in part, on the number of copies of a particular type of kringle encoded in the gene for apolipoprotein(a). People carry anywhere from 1 to more than 40 copies; the fewer the copies, the smaller the particle, and the higher the Lp(a) level. That is because liver cells seem to have an easier time producing and secreting the smaller particles.

Researchers are still trying to unpack how that structural difference affects the particle’s function and its role in cardiovascular disease. Particle for particle, Lp(a) carries six times the risk that LDL does. That could be because it’s more effective at depositing cholesterol on artery walls, or because it promotes inflammation, which can contribute to plaque deposition. But Nordestgaard thinks it has more to do with the impact of Lp(a) on blood clotting. The particle’s tail might make it more difficult for the body to break down clots, which could lead to larger blockages.

Many countries recommend that adults get their Lp(a) levels tested at least once. European atherosclerosis and cardiology societies first recommended that physicians test Lp(a) levels in 2019, and earlier this year, those in the United States followed suit. Because there is no approved therapy for lowering Lp(a), the standard of care for people with high levels is to aggressively reduce other risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

But high Lp(a) levels don’t always cause problems. Bhatia says that sometimes older people have high Lp(a) levels but never have a cardiovascular event. “And sometimes we don’t even see plaque when we look with imaging,” he says. “It may just be that it’s the overall picture of risk, and that Lp(a) is just one piece of that bigger puzzle.”

By HARRY BAMFORTH, LIVE SPORTS COVERAGE REPORTER

Published: 14:16 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 19:08 EDT, 4 November 2026

Tenerife striker Jesus de ​Miguel has been admitted to intensive care after collapsing during a Spanish second division clash with Andorra on Monday.

The 30-year-old is in stable condition, the club has confirmed, after a horrifying collision with goalkeeper ‌Jesus Owono led to the fixture being abandoned deep into stoppage time with the scores level at 2-2.

A club statement read: 'CD Tenerife player Jesús de Miguel is admitted to the ICU at the University Hospital of Nuestra Señora de Candelaria, stable despite the severity of his condition.

'The medical services at said hospital will be present and will report when there are updates.'

De Miguel is believed to have suffered a cardiac arrest while being transported to hospital and had to be revived inside the ambulance, according to Spanish media outlet Marca.

It has also been reported that while the Spaniard is stable, he remains unconscious.

Jesus de ​Miguel (pictured playing for former club Castellon) has been taken to intensive care

Tenerife's De ​Miguel was wiped out by Jesus Owono during a Spanish second tier match

The game had entered the seventh minute of stoppage time when De Miguel looked set to race away on the counter-attack for Tenerife in search of a winner.

As he watched a long ball drop into his path, the striker appeared to be struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line.

After initially rolling around on the floor, De Miguel became motionless, and medical staff rushed onto the pitch to attend to him.

De Miguel was seen to for over five minutes while his team-mates were visibly distressed, with some appearing to be in tears.

Owono was initially given a red card for the challenge before the decision was soon taken by the referee to abandon the fixture.

The stadium has been in complete silence while De Miguel was being treated, but as he was taken off the pitch the striker was given a standing ovation by the crowd.

De Miguel was rushed to hospital following the incident after appearing motionless on the pitch

After being taken to an ambulance on a stretcher, there is believed to have been an approximate 15-minute wait before they made their way to the hospital.

Andorra also released a statement, which read: 'We want to send all our strength and best wishes to Jesus de Miguel after the serious incident suffered during today's match.

'We hope he recovers soon. A very strong hug to the player, his family and Tenerife.'

Despite remaining unconcsious in intensive care the player is believed to be 'breathing on his own'.

#1411. Chinese doctoral students in clinical medicine can graduate without a thesis — more degrees to follow

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Postgraduate students studying clinical medicine in China have the option to graduate with a practical achievement, such as an analysis of a special clinical case, rather than a thesis.Credit: Xie Shangguo/VCG via Getty

Master’s and doctoral candidates in some clinical medicine degrees in China can now graduate with a ‘practical achievement’ instead of a thesis. This is the second field to open such a pathway. Since 2024, master’s and PhD students in engineering have been allowed to graduate from universities across China after developing a new product, technique, project or installation.

On 22 October, a team of government-appointed education advisers released draft policy documents setting out the rules for the graduation pathway for students pursuing a professional master’s or doctoral degree in clinical medicine — both are three-year courses typically taken by medical graduates and practising physicians.

In China, professional postgraduate courses focus on training students to solve problems in a particular line of work rather than developing research skills, as they would in an academic degree. The rules state that students have the option to graduate with a practical achievement, such as an analysis of a special clinical case or an investigation into a problem facing medical institutes.

Postgraduate courses in translation, agriculture, accounting and arts are expected to introduce similar pathways to graduation, according to China’s Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council, a government body driving reforms for postgraduate education.

These reforms are a step in the right direction, because students preparing for professional careers should be trained and assessed in ways that reflect those careers, says Futao Huang, a researcher of higher-education policy at Hiroshima University in Higashihiroshima, Japan. “The real challenge is to develop credible, transparent and profession-specific standards for assessing practical achievements,” Huang adds.

For students pursuing a professional degree in clinical medicine, the new graduation pathway means that they can be assessed on the contribution that their research will bring to patients and society, says Zhou Feifei, a spinal surgeon at Peking University Third Hospital in Beijing. “This will encourage them to find problems in real life and to address the problem using a scientific way,” he adds.

One of Zhou’s students, Tie Dazhao, was the first person to graduate with a ‘practical PhD’ in clinical medicine in June, having been selected as a pilot case in 2023. Tie developed an artificial-intelligence-empowered software programme that can help physicians to classify a type of rare spinal condition and recommend suitable treatment strategies to them, says Zhou.

Individual universities are encouraged to form their own policies on training practical postgraduate students and what requirements students must meet to graduate, says Liping Duan, chief physician of gastroenterology at Peking University Third Hospital and a member of a national advisory committee tasked with formulating the policy for clinical medicine. One of the biggest challenges will be creating a uniform standard to assess practical achievements, Duan says. “What works for cardiology may not work for dermatology, for example,” she adds.

How to control the quality of the achievements will also be important, Duan says. “Some people may mistakenly think that graduation has become easier now that students can choose not to write a thesis.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03480-7

#1410. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1409. Barry Sees Blues Beat Newcastle Again

Thierno Barry's eighth goal of the season proved enough for Everton to beat Newcastle for the second time in the space of four days in a 1-0 win at St James' Park.

Having triumphed 3-1 in the Carabao Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Blues left the North East with three Premier League points this time around.

Following a dominant first-half display, Everton got their reward four minutes after the restart when keeper Lukas Hornicek spilled Tyrique George's low shot, allowing Barry to tap home from a yard out.

That proved decisive to continue the Toffees' fine recent record at St James' Park – with a third victory on the trot – as David Moyes' men moved up to seventh in the Premier League table.

Moyes made two changes from the team that beat the Magpies 3-1 in the Carabao Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium four days earlier – Jarrad Branthwaite returning from a concussion protocol and Harrison Armstrong preferred to Hayden Hackney in central midfield.

Branthwaite partnering James Tarkowski in central defence saw Jake O'Brien switch to right-back, with Merlin Röhl getting the nod ahead of Tyler Dibling to play in front of the Irishman.

Buoyed by their success over Matthias Jaissle's team on Merseyside last week, the Blues made an excellent start and did not look back in a dominant first half that had everything but a deserved opener.

Röhl was the first to threaten when he collected a pass from Thierno Barry and drove a rising first-time angled shot narrowly over the bar, before Barry failed to get a clean connection from seven yards out after Jarrad Branthwaite headed down Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's free-kick into the striker's path.

Everton then had two more opportunities to edge ahead in two minutes of first-half added-time. Dewsbury-Hall's glorious curling cross from the left edge of the area narrowly evaded O'Brien lurking at the back post. And the Toffees' No.8 turned provider again seconds later, getting the freedom down the left flank to cut back to Armstrong, who screwed his first-time finish wide when well placed from 12 yards out.

Thankfully, the Toffees did not have to wait long to find the back of the net after the restart. Four minutes into the second half, James Garner slid George in through the left channel and, when the winger's shot squeezed through the hands of Hornicek, Barry was left with the simple task of tucking home from a yard out.

With the wind in their sails, Everton went close to a second as Branthwaite's header was turned over the bar by Hornicek, before the Newcastle keeper did the same with Dewsbury-Hall's whipped shot from 25 yards out.

And from the resulting corner, Garner picked out O'Brien at the back post to nod down a goalbound header which Hornicek did well to turn behind.

Having done little to worry Jordan Pickford up until the hour mark, the hosts went so close to levelling when substitute Yoane Wissa nodded into Anthony Elanga at the back post who squeezed a finish under the England No.1 but, thankfully, the ball rolled along the line before being booted clear by Tarkowski.

As the inevitable Newcastle pressure grew trying to find a leveller, substitute Jacob Ramsey hit a volley from the edge of the area with 11 minutes remaining that crept inches past the left-hand post.

Then, as eight minutes of injury-time approached, Wissa looked to apply a finish from close range only to be denied by the legs of Pickford.

And that was to prove crucial as Everton saw out the closing stages, Ramsey being given his marching orders with seconds remaining after picking up two quick yellow cards for late tackles on substitute Hackney and then Armstrong.

#1408. How democracy depends on science — and must protect it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Martin Kahanec is a professor at the Central European University, Vienna, Austria, and affiliated with the Central European Labor Studies Institute and Bratislava University of Economics and Business, Bratislava, Slovakia, and the European University Institute, Florence, Italy.

Naomi Ellemers is a distinguished professor at Utrecht University, Utrecht, the Netherlands.

Adam Izdebski is a professor of human ecology at the Institute of Advanced Studies, Nicolaus Copernicus University, Toruń, Poland.

Rafal M. Łukasik is a professor of chemical engineering and the director of the Łukasiewicz Research Network, Industrial Chemistry Institute, Warsaw, Poland.

Dimitra Simeonidou is a professor of high-performance networks and the director of the Smart Internet Lab at the University of Bristol, Bristol, UK.

Rémy Slama is a senior investigator and professor at INSERM and ENS-PSL, Paris, France.

Mangala Srinivas is a professor of cell biology and immunology at Wageningen University and Research, Wageningen, the Netherlands.

For scientists, thoughts about democracy can feel distant from their work. Yet, around the world, governments are limiting academic freedom and interfering with decisions about what research is funded and who performs it1. Some scientists are also facing politically motivated interference and attacks2.

Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities

Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities

As members of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, we feel it is urgent to address this concern and that we have a responsibility to make scientists’ voices heard.

Science and democracy are often viewed as distinct — science as a source of discovery, expertise and innovation and democracy as a set of institutions, rules and procedures. But, in reality, the two are intertwined3.

Science is an essential backbone of democracy. In an increasingly complex and fast-changing world, people need access to verified information and independent knowledge to make informed decisions4,5. Research aids that by generating reliable evidence and fostering critical enquiry, thus enabling a plurality of views to be discussed and creating conditions in which societies can learn from experience.

In May, Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, asked us to provide advice on how science can strengthen the European Union’s democratic functioning and resilience.

Independently of that process, here we put forward three pillars through which science enables democracy: establishing shared factual baselines, aiding trust in institutions and providing tools to adapt policies and organizations in response to changing circumstances.

The first pillar relates to protecting the foundations and integrity of information on which democratic judgements, collective deliberation and, ultimately, action depend.

Democratic societies constantly confront questions for which there are no simple, best or permanent answers. Scientific institutions help societies to navigate changing realities by creating procedures for gathering evidence about the current situation, past trends, probable outcomes or management options; assessing impacts; communicating disagreement; quantifying uncertainties; and updating conclusions in light of new findings.

Artificial-intelligence and other digital platforms are changing how people find information, develop opinions and take part in public life6. This not only provides opportunities for broadening participation and increasing transparency, but also produces intensified, increasingly complex or fresh risks, including of misinformation, manipulation, bias, polarization and fragmentation6,7. Moreover, these developments amplify the disproportionate influence of a small number of powerful technology companies and their leaders8, including their ability to ‘manufacture doubt’ and shape public opinion9,10.

How to get science back into policymaking

How to get science back into policymaking

The challenge goes further than just correcting people’s misconceptions. Disinformation is often rooted in social networks, reinforced by emotions and group identities and used deliberately for political purposes5,7. It spreads through networks of people connected by identity, grievance or distrust. These vulnerabilities can be exploited by individuals seeking to advance political or economic interests9, thereby undermining democratic institutions, deepening divisions and fostering instability6.

Citizens have legitimate concerns about economic restructuring, regional inequities, how migration is governed, technological changes, ageing populations, climate risks and geopolitical instability. People might lose trust in democratic institutions, especially if they feel they are not being heard, do not understand why something changed, think they are treated unfairly or see the fabric of their communities being disrupted11. This might create vulnerabilities that can be exploited through disinformation and political manipulation5.

For this reason, scientific approaches to democratic resilience must go beyond fact-checking and include the design of effective channels for science communication and information sharing, as well as opportunities for meaningful public participation and informed deliberation4,12. These should include transparent data sources in digital platforms; independent media; strong safeguards against foreign interference; secure information infrastructures; independent monitoring and assurance of algorithmic systems; and improved understanding of how the expanding use of AI tools might shape democratic discourse and outcomes13.

The second pillar refers to the legitimacy of expertise and the trustworthiness of institutions. Democratic governance can be thought of as a shared societal capacity to understand complex realities, to deliberate across differences and to act together in the face of social, economic and technological transformations and uncertainty4,6. Its resilience rests on organizations that sustain public trust and active citizenship, and on people’s capacity to participate meaningfully in deliberation and collective problem-solving4,14.

Institutions that are informed by scientific evidence and guided by scientific principles are better equipped than others to make effective, transparent and accountable decisions, strengthening public trust in democracy11. During a pandemic or other crisis, or in anticipation of such events, authorities can reinforce trust by explaining clearly how scientific evidence, including any limitations and uncertainties, informs their decisions.

But for science to strengthen democracy, researchers must be trusted, too15,16. Moreover, the legitimacy of expertise has become increasingly contested over the past few years in Europe and elsewhere5,15.

Scientific advice is subjected to politicization in many countries, with consensual insights and clear evidence (such as on climate change) being dismissed as ‘just another opinion’ or as being driven by a political agenda5,9. Public trust in expertise has become polarized along political lines5,15. Some officials and politicians might support specific strands of science, for instance, by promoting individual researchers or a few disciplines selectively. Such favouritism has implications for funding.

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

This ‘divide and rule’ approach to science is often tacitly accepted by the academic community, with many institutions preferring to stay silent rather than run the risk of their budgets being cut. The dilution of scientific knowledge in an ever-increasing flow of online information, often promoted by individuals with vested interests seeking to influence public decisions, can also render impartial scientific evidence and advice less visible.

Expertise strengthens democratic legitimacy when it is transparent, diverse, independent and open to scrutiny — as prescribed by the rules of science. But it weakens legitimacy when it is perceived as opaque, unclear, politicized, elitist or disconnected from people’s lived experiences.

Ensuring that expert information is democratically legitimate requires institutions and mechanisms that not only structure the interaction between science, policy and society, but also protect organizations’ separate, independent roles, manage conflicts of interests and prevent undue influence.

Crucially, not every engagement with science carries equal weight. Impartial access to scientific knowledge is most reliably secured through a cross-disciplinary and diverse group of experts. By contrast, the opinion of a single scientist might result in partial understanding (highlighting a particular disciplinary perspective) or reliance on a dissenting voice that differs from the majority view. High-level expert groups, which engage directly with senior decision makers, can identify a broader range of potential concerns. They can better understand the wider implications of policy challenges to provide relevant scientific evidence and advice, yet maintain independence in their analysis, conclusions and recommendations.

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Public institutions should ensure that scientists who provide advice can do so independently and that they are free to publish their findings. This generally requires stable public funding of research1. Cuts to public science budgets can increase scientists’ dependence on a narrow range of funders, including private and commercial organizations or institutions linked to other countries. Their funding decisions could reflect strategic or political interests and might create actual or perceived conflicts of interest if appropriate transparency guidelines and safeguards are not in place.

The European Commission’s science-advice framework provides a useful example of how scientific independence can be achieved. It combines topic-specific evidence reviews by multidisciplinary expert groups with independent policy recommendations from its seven chief scientific advisers. The advisers are supported by a permanent secretariat that helps them to align scientific advice with policy needs and safeguards the independence of the advisory process. This mechanism also includes rules on transparency and the disclosure of advisers’ conflicts of interest (see go.nature.com/4jndrg).

Scientific expert groups should be able to propose topics, identify questions and communicate evidence, uncertainties and policy options to decision makers and the public independently.

But trust depends on people having the opportunity to engage with science, too. Scientific literacy, civic education, public engagement with research and access to reliable information are all essential and need to be supported by public and educational institutions. Opportunities for science education are a public good and should be accessible to all.

#1407. Seamus Coleman Interviews Newcastle PotM Dewsbury-Hall

Seamus Coleman interviewed former Toffees teammate, and close friend, Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall after Everton's 1-0 victory over Newcastle United at St James' Park on Monday night.

The Blues saw off the Magpies for the second time in four days courtesy of Thierno Barry's 49th-minute winner to move up to seventh in the Premier League.

Player of the match in Thursday's 3-1 Carabao Cup success, Dewsbury-Hall did it again in the North East with another outstanding midfield display to further push his claims for an England call-up later this month.

And after the full-time whistle at St James' Park, Everton's No.8 spoke to his ex-Blues captain Coleman, with the Toffees icon a studio guest on Sky Sports' Monday Night Football...

That must mean a lot when you get a hug like that from the Gaffer?

Yeah, you don’t get many of them off the Gaffer so I must have done alright. What a win. I’m really, really happy. It’s been a great four days.

Really, really happy. I thought that was one of our best performances of the season. It’s a tough place to come, especially after beating them four days before so they were going to come back at us with extra impetus to win the game. I thought we played really well, we stopped their momentum. We scored a nice goal and the most important thing is a clean sheet, so happy days!

Did you talk beforehand that if you did start well, you could get the crowd to turn?

For sure. We know they want to start really well at home, so if we can try to counteract that and start well, it’s only going to go in our favour. I thought at the start it was us pressing and pushing for a goal. We had some good opportunities and that set the tone for the rest of the game.

SEAMUS: I saw you getting a hug like that from the manager every day! We spoke in the week about how important this week was for Everton. You’ve stepped up massively for Everton. I thought you were the best player on the pitch tonight. A great week...

I thought this week was massive for us. I think if we had two different results, it’d be a much different feel around the Club but we’re in the quarter-finals of the cup and in the top half of the league. It’s been a top week and I’m really happy.

Are you and the Club both striving for more?

Overall, it’s been a positive 18 months for the Club with everything that’s gone on, with the new stadium and we got so close to getting in Europe last season. I came to this club because it’s a massive, massive club. It’s a sleeping giant of the English game so I really want to do something here, win some silverware or give the fans something to scream about, because they’re unbelievable.

You see them home and away. I’m really happy we’re through to the next round. I want to keep pushing and pushing. I’m not here to just go through the motions and finish mid-table. No, I want to push for something, because I’m coming into the prime years of my career and I want to show and look back on my career and say I’m done something for a massive football club.

We’ll have to wait and see! It’s about time Seamus stops asking me to play for Ireland! It is what it is. I’ll just keep trying to put in good performances like that and whatever happens, happens. I’ve said in the past, if I’m performing for my football club, it only gives me a better chance of playing for my country. And I’ll keep doing that until I hang my boots up.

#1406. Dermot Desmond must attend AGM and engage with supporters, insists Celtic Fans Collective

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:14 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 17:16 EDT, 2 November 2026

The Celtic Fans Collective has demanded that Dermot Desmond attends the forthcoming Annual General Meeting to answer questions on how the club is being run on his watch.

The Irish billionaire, the club’s largest single shareholder, has been absent from the shareholder meeting for the past 20 years, latterly deploying his son, Ross, to attend as his representative.

Tensions between the fan base and the board – and Desmond in particular – have escalated across the past two years, primarily as a consequence of growing concern over the way the club is operating off the field and the team’s regression in Europe.

Last month, the feud took a new twist when masked supporters, who were part of the Collective, threw tennis balls at Desmond as he participated in the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews.

That resulted in the club releasing a strongly worded statement criticising the incident and ceasing all engagement with the group.

However, the umbrella body, which represents 168 supporters’ organisations, feels it’s incumbent on Desmond to break with tradition by turning up in person at this year’s annual meeting – the date of which has yet to be announced.

Irish billionaire Dermot Desmond has been absent from Celtic's AGM for the past 20 years

Supporters want to question Celtic's largest single shareholder about how the club is run

It said in a statement: ‘For 20 years, Dermot Desmond has not attended Celtic’s Annual General Meeting, despite wielding considerable influence over the direction and decision-making of our club.

‘Although only a minority shareholder, Desmond appears to exercise influence far beyond his shareholding. With that influence comes a responsibility to be accountable.

‘We call on Dermot Desmond to publicly commit to attending the 2026 AGM in person and answer questions about his role in the running of Celtic Football Club.

‘Sending his son, another representative or a prepared statement in his place is no substitute for attending personally.’

The statement went on to reference the chaotic scenes at last year’s meeting which ended with then chairman Peter Lawwell cutting the meeting short after protesters brandishing red cards shouted down directors.

Ross Desmond had previously read out a statement on his father’s behalf in which he hit out at the ‘destructive and cynical’ criticism of club executives and branded some fans ‘bullies’.

Desmond is escorted off after tennis balls were flung at him in the Dunhill Links Championship

‘The decision by Peter Lawwell to prematurely conclude last year’s AGM left a clear impression among supporters that the board had taken an opportunity to avoid scrutiny,’ it added.

‘Responsibility for how that meeting was conducted and ultimately concluded rests entirely with the board.

‘This year, however, the focus must be firmly on scrutiny rather than protest. There is a clear understanding across the support that the AGM must provide the opportunity for important questions to be put directly to those running the club, without allowing scrutiny to be evaded once again.

‘Celtic supporters have repeatedly sought meaningful dialogue and a more constructive relationship with the club.

‘At a time when fans want to see decisive leadership, a public commitment from Dermot Desmond to attend the AGM in good faith would be an important demonstration of his willingness to engage directly with supporters and shareholders.’

The date of last year’s meeting was confirmed on October 28. Shareholders must be given 21 days’ notice of this year’s event.

#1405. Newcastle look like a team bereft of energy and inspiration under Matthias Jaissle - as Everton continue to thrive without Jack Grealish after another impressive victory, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 17:16 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 18:11 EDT, 2 November 2026

Jack Grealish was pictured enjoying a cracking night out in Newcastle last year. Here, his Everton team-mates had just as good a time, albeit in a far more sober state.

The Manchester City loanee was left at home after last week’s ‘breach of club discipline’. At least, home is where the club hoped he would be.

And, if he was, Grealish would have watched Everton record a deserved win. He might even have raised a toast, so accomplished an away performance was this.

David Moyes had dropped the winger for last Thursday’s 3-1 win over Newcastle in the Carabao Cup after he missed training following another alleged night on the town. And again, without him, they were too good for Matthias Jaissle’s sorry and directionless Newcastle.

It is the Toon Army, rather, in need of a bender right now. They really aren’t very good - no shots on target before injury-time - and it is remarkable to think they would have gone seventh with victory. That position is now occupied by Everton, who were more skilful and more savvy from start to finish and won thanks to Thierno Barry’s goal just after the break. The scoreline was not a reflection of their superiority.

Jaissle said: ‘We were not brave enough to break the line and play on the ground. We saw it in training, but there was almost nothing to see from these aspects in the game.

Everton, who were more skilful and more savvy from start to finish, won thanks to Thierno Barry’s goal just after the break

Jaissle’s promise has been a team who hunt in packs, yet they were hiding en mass here

‘We have a clear identity of how we want to play - to bring the opposition in stressful situations high in the pitch. We spoke about creating one-on-one situations. The plan was not to play the long balls.’

The opening half hour had been a side-show in two managers betraying varying degrees of frustration. Jaissle buried his fist in his palm every time Everton played through his team at will. And Moyes muttered expletives when his side were unable to take advantage. It was clear he sensed this was there to be won. It was less clear how they would achieve that when Barry was swiping at fresh air six yards from goal.

Newcastle (4-2-3-1): Hornicek 4; Dedic 4, Schar 5, Burn 5, Hall 5; Gonzalez 4 (Steur 64, 6), Joelinton 4 (Ramsey 76, 5); Elanga 4 (Murphy 76, 5) Willock 4 (Wissa 64, 5), Barnes 5; Osula 4.

Everton (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; O’Brien 7, Tarkowski 7, Branthwaite 7, Mykolenko 7; Garner 7, Armstrong 7; Rohl 6, DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 6; Barry 7.

By the 28th minute, the home fans were booing after yet another aimless long ball. Vertical football, Jaissle has called it, getting the ball forward quickly. Yet more boos on the whistle for half-time told you the locals fear they are going backwards. Everton’s Harrison Armstrong, the half’s brightest midfielder, had only just swiped wide from 12 yards when he should have scored, and that would have been deserved.

The Toon Army were soon cheering, when a fella in jeans kicked a ball through a hole to win a trip to Las Vegas. It was the first effort on target by anyone on the field all evening. Newcastle’s first-half woe was summed up by one free-kick, worked short, that was then chipped straight out of play by Amar Dedic. Jaissle shot to his dugout to watch a replay of what had gone wrong - someone should have told him such footage could not be re-shown pre watershed.

The first effort on target brought the first goal in the 49th minute, and it was no surprise when it came Everton’s way. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall played the sort of pass of which Newcastle were seemingly incapable - low, incisive and accurate - and that set Tyrique George away. His shot was not particularly hard, but then Lukas Hornicek’s attempt to save it was not particularly convincing. As the ball squirmed through his grasp, Barry was quickest to follow up for a tap-in. Newcastle appealed offsides against both George and the scorer, but the truth was that Everton’s players were just sharper in every phase. The time afforded to the excellent Dewsbury-Hall to pick that pass was also a scandal.

Jaissle’s promise has been a team who hunt in packs. They were hiding en mass here. The head coach looked to his bench and called for the popular midfielder Sean Steur. The Dutch teenager’s popularity has been enhanced by him not being in the side of late. The cheer for his introduction, as replacement for the leaden-booted Nico Gonzalez, was almost as big as for the sharp-shooter in Levi’s.

Immediately, Steur impacted. From one smart pass to Harvey Barnes the winger crossed and Anthony Elanga almost stole in to score at the far post. The Geordies have been right to call for his involvement in a team so void of inspiration and positive energy.

It was not long, however, before a chorus of ‘attack, attack, attack’ emerged from the Gallowgate End, and that is never a good sign. Substitute Jacob Ramsey was then sent off for a second booking to compound the home misery.

Meanwhile, the fan bound for Vegas was probably checking for the next flight.

Matthias Jaissle accused his Newcastle players of failing to follow his plan for the match against Everton – claiming they played long balls against his wishes.

The under-pressure boss, whose side have lost four from five and sit 13th in the Premier League after Monday night’s 1-0 defeat at St James’s Park, saw frontman Will Osula isolated as his team failed to register a shot on target until the 85th minute.

‘There is big frustration and disappointment,’ said the German, who replaced Eddie Howe this summer.

‘We could not transfer what we saw in the week, training in a high level. Since the start of the game, not much was seen. That is difficult to understand.

‘We were not brave enough to break the line and play on the ground. We saw it in training, but there was almost nothing to see from these aspects in the game. In possession, this was not the level we wanted to see.

‘If you just play long balls, it’s not the style Osula prefers and that was not the plan.

'We need to analyse this in depth, why we could not start the game how we planned. I’m responsible for that, to make it work.

Newcastle frontman Will Osula was unable to make an impression on the game

Matthias Jaissle's side have now lost four of their last five games

Thierno Barry’s second-half goal inflicted Newcastle’s second defeat by Everton in the space of five days, following the 3-1 loss on Merseyside in the Carabao Cup last Thursday.

#1401. Trump’s executive order on women’s health feels like déjà vu

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alina Salganicoff is senior vice-president and director for women’s health policy at KFF in San Francisco, California.

To improve women’s health and quality of life, more research is needed on conditions that exclusively or disproportionately affect women.Credit: Good Brigade/Getty

The five-year survival rate for breast cancer in the United States rose from 76% in 1975 to 94% in 2023. This was no accident; it was the result of sustained investment in research, and it shows how remarkable progress can be achieved when women’s health is prioritized.

Women are talking about menopause — health systems must listen

Women are talking about menopause — health systems must listen

Breast cancer research funding at the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) dwarfs what is spent on any other condition that exclusively or disproportionately affects women. Unfortunately, the US national research enterprise has not adequately advanced the treatment and prevention of many other conditions that lead to premature mortality, disability or diminished quality of life for women.

In October, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order creating a task force on women’s health and directing the NIH to establish a Women’s Health Division in an existing institute. This could be a meaningful step. But what comes next? White House attention and support is important, but making good progress will require expanded funding from the US Congress and structural change at the NIH.

The country has been here before. In 1993, then-president Bill Clinton signed the NIH Revitalization Act, a law that was intended to address gaps in women’s health research and formally established the Office of Research on Women’s Health (ORWH). Two years ago, then-president Joe Biden launched an all-of-government initiative and established an NIH-wide task force to improve women’s health research and redirect federal funds to gaps in it. Biden also called for Congress to allocate US$12 billion to support NIH research into women’s health, but that funding was not included in the final appropriation.

There is no question that NIH-supported research has helped to improve women’s health, but large gaps persist. Endometriosis, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, uterine fibroids, menopause and ovarian and endometrial cancers are all examples of conditions affecting women that have been poorly funded and underprioritized.

Neglecting sex and gender in research is a public-health risk

Neglecting sex and gender in research is a public-health risk

Furthermore, the understanding of human biology and disease has historically been based on male models — whether laboratory animals or human participants. Even when women are included in clinical trials, those who are pregnant or lactating are generally excluded, and sex-specific analyses are still too rare. There is also a lack of understanding of many fundamental aspects of female physiology, and of sex differences in conditions such as migraines, autoimmune diseases, Alzheimer’s disease and depression, as well as the safe management of health concerns during pregnancy.

As a policy researcher, I have spent much of my career focused on the barriers that limit women’s access to care. I have also been part of committees that develop recommendations to shape US insurance coverage, and seen at first hand how research gaps affect the guidelines for women’s health conditions. In 2024, I had the privilege of co-chairing a congressionally mandated consensus committee at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine tasked with assessing the status of women’s health research at the NIH and making recommendations to improve it.

#1400. Michael Carrick's next nightmare: How Aston Villa misfit Donyell Malen became Europe's hottest striker... as Roma star looks to pile on the misery for Man United in Champions League

Published: 02:00 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 04:31 EDT, 3 November 2026

It’s been a brutal start to the season for Manchester United, who are winless in nine games on the spin.

And as Michael Carrick fights to save his job, they must now find a way to deal with the most potent forward in Europe’s top five leagues.

Donyell Malen, the reinvented centre-forward, has caught fire in Italy, a world away from the talented but unspectacular winger who left Aston Villa.

The 27-year-old arrives at Old Trafford on Tuesday as Europe’s most prolific striker, with Roma unbeaten in Serie A. Villa let him go for just £25million.

Roma are contenders in Serie A, and Malen’s goals are the biggest reason why.

The Dutchman has totalled 22 goals in 2026. That is more than any player in the big five leagues, including newly crowned Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane.

At Villa, it never quite happened for him. Malen arrived from Borussia Dortmund in January 2025 - the same window as Jhon Duran’s departure - but he spent most of his minutes out wide and never nailed down a starting place. Neither wing suited a player miscast as a pacey wideman.

Donyell Malen has scored 22 league goals in 2026 - more than even Harry Kane

Malen played just one and a half seasons at Villa Park, scoring 10 goals in 46 games

The Dutchman scored just 10 goals in 46 games at Villa Park, which hid his quality. He grew into his second season and was named Villa’s Player of the Month in November; but two months later, he was sold.

'It was my decision,' Malen told Italian media. 'I wanted to play and be part of a team where I could take the field every weekend and play an important role. At that stage, I didn’t feel important, so I think I made the best choice.

'Today I feel I’m in the right place with the right people. The coach and my teammates show a lot of confidence in me, and together, all of this is helping me become the player I dreamed of being.'

The signs of improvement were here before this summer's World Cup, though Malen  could not find the net despite starting all three Netherlands group games. Brian Brobbey was the side's focal point, returning Malen to a supporting role alongside Cody Gakpo.

It was a surprise to Dutch fans, who remember the centre forward terrorising defences at PSV, where he scored 19 goals and added eight assists in his final full season in 2020-21.

Roma boss Gian Piero Gasperini, who joined the club the previous summer, had moved Malen into a role he had not played in years: striker. The result was an outrageous 14 goals in 18 games to finish the season.

Malen has struck up a potent partnership with Paulo Dybala

Malen has rewarded his manager’s faith by helping secure Champions League football, a level the club have not reached since 2018.

Position is only part of the story. Once forced to create chances, Malen now finishes them. Argentine wizards Matias Soule and Paulo Dybala are his accomplices in a stellar front three, feeding him the best service in Europe.

Starting alongside Dybala, Malen got off to the perfect start to the season with a hat-trick in a 4-0 home win over Fiorentina.

'Getting off to such a good start by scoring a hat-trick was crucial,' he said. 'As a team we were strong and connected, and I immediately had a very good feeling. We can build on moments like these and do something special. Paulo and I clicked immediately.'

When Dybala’s constant niggles strike, new signing Rodrigo Mora has proved more than an adequate stand-in, helping to spearhead Roma’s title charge.

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.
